entities.name: CONCACAF
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football (CONCACAF), founded on September 18, 1961, in Mexico City, is a pivotal governing body in international soccer, overseeing competitions involving 41 member associations across North America, Central America, and the Caribbean. As a cornerstone of the global football community, its establishment marked a significant moment in the organization of the sport, influencing how football was played and governed in its regions and contributing to a growing sense of unity and identity among member nations.

Key achievements of CONCACAF include the creation of the CONCACAF Gold Cup, first held in 1991, which has become a premier international tournament for national teams in the region. The body has also played an essential role in the development of soccer infrastructure and youth programs, notably through initiatives such as the CONCACAF Champions League, which showcases club-level competition. Furthermore, the organization has been instrumental in enhancing the visibility and professionalism of soccer in member countries, contributing to the sport's economic growth and cultural significance in these regions.

The legacy of CONCACAF extends beyond the field, as it has fostered greater collaboration among its member nations, allowing for shared resources, talent development, and cultural exchange. This cooperative spirit promotes not only sporting excellence but also economic ties and social connections across borders. The organization has also been a vital player in the global soccer governance landscape, influencing FIFA's policies and practices, particularly in relation to commercial rights and tournament scheduling.
